nameStory: Despite its name, Coastal Plain Blue-eyed Grass isn't a grass at all – it's actually a member of the iris family! The 'blue-eyed' part comes from its tiny but brilliant blue flowers with bright yellow centers that really do look like little eyes peering up at you. The 'coastal plain' refers to its preference for the flat, sandy areas near the coast where it thrives.
description: Coastal Plain Blue-eyed Grass is a delicate little plant that forms small clumps of narrow, grass-like leaves rising 6-12 inches tall. Its most striking feature is its small but intensely blue flowers, each about half an inch across, that seem to glow against the green foliage. The flowers have six pointed petals arranged in a star shape with bright yellow centers, blooming on slender stems that rise just above the leaves. This charming wildflower creates modest colonies in sandy soils, often hiding in plain sight among actual grasses.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant blue, six-petaled flowers about 1/2 inch across with bright yellow centers and three prominent stamens. Each flower lasts only one day, opening in morning sunshine and closing by afternoon.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, grass-like leaves that are flat and sword-shaped, growing in small tufts. Feel stiff and slightly rough to the touch, unlike the softer texture of true grasses.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, neat clumps 6-12 inches tall, often growing in scattered colonies. Flowering stems are thin and wiry, slightly taller than the leaves.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round capsules develop after flowers fade, splitting open to release tiny dark seeds. Capsules feel papery when dry.

habitat: Found in sandy, well-drained soils of coastal plains, particularly in pine barrens, sandy fields, and woodland edges. In New England, it's most common in the southeastern coastal areas where sandy soils dominate. Often grows alongside other coastal plain specialists like little bluestem grass and wild lupine.

seasonality.spring: New grass-like leaves emerge as small green tufts, easily overlooked among other emerging vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from late May through July, when the brilliant blue flowers are most visible in morning sunshine.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, leaves may begin to yellow but often remain somewhat green through early fall.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, with only dried seed stalks potentially visible above snow.

funFact: Each tiny flower opens for just one day and only when the sun is shining – on cloudy days, you might walk right past a patch and never know the flowers are there because they stay tightly closed!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with actual grasses when not in bloom, but the stiff, iris-like leaves and the fact that it grows in distinct clumps (not spreading runners like grass) are good clues. When blooming, the blue flowers immediately distinguish it from true grasses, which have inconspicuous wind-pollinated flowers.
contextualKnowledge: The name causes endless confusion since this plant looks like grass but is actually closely related to garden irises. It's part of a group called 'blue-eyed grasses' that includes several similar species, all of which are iris family members masquerading as grasses.
compareHints: Coastal Plain Blue-eyed Grass is distinguished from other New England blue-eyed grasses by its preference for sandy coastal soils and its slightly more robust growth habit. Eastern Blue-eyed Grass is very similar but typically found in different habitats, while Strict Blue-eyed Grass has more upright, stiffer stems and Narrow-leaved Blue-eyed Grass has even thinner leaves and smaller flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Strict blue-eyed grass is very similar to narrow-leaved blue-eyed grass and is sometimes considered the same species.
Narrow-leaved blue-eyed grass has the thinnest leaves among New England's blue-eyed grasses, typically less than 1/8 inch wide.
Eastern blue-eyed grass can be tricky to distinguish from its close relatives without careful observation.

Among New England's blue-eyed grasses, needle-tipped blue-eyed-grass stands out for its truly sharp leaf tips that can pierce skin, while strict blue-eyed grass and narrow-leaved blue-eyed grass have pointed but not needle-sharp leaves.
